items.title: EDF, SOFTEX and the two clocks an exporter lives by
items.core_explanation_md:
**What is declared**: goods go on the **Export Declaration Form (EDF)**; software sent in non-physical form goes on the **SOFTEX** form. A few cases are **exempt** from declaring (listed in Regulation 4 of the Export Regulations), but the exporter must still **realise and repatriate the proceeds**.

**Clock 1: submit documents within 21 days** of the export. If late, the authorised dealer may still handle them **without prior RBI approval** if it is satisfied with the reasons.

**Clock 2: realise the money within nine months** of the export, for all exporters including SEZ units, status holders, EOUs and units in EHTPs, STPs and BTPs.
- **Warehouse abroad**: proceeds within **fifteen months** of shipment.
- **Bharat Mart**: **nine months** from the date of sale of the goods from the warehouse.

The period went to **fifteen months** in November 2025 and was **restored to nine months** on 5 June 2026, so **nine months** applies at the exam cut-off.

items.title: When the money is late: extending the realisation period
items.core_explanation_md:
The exporter applies to the authorised dealer. The bank may extend by **up to six months at a time**, whatever the invoice value, if **all** of these hold:

1. The exports are **not under investigation** by the Directorate of Enforcement, the CBI or other agencies.
2. The bank is satisfied the delay is for **reasons beyond the exporter's control**.
3. The exporter **declares** the proceeds will be realised in the extended period.
4. If the extension goes **beyond one year** from export, the exporter's **total outstanding** is within **USD 1 million or 10% of average export realisation in the last three financial years, whichever is higher**.

If the exporter has **sued the buyer abroad**, extension may be given **whatever the amount**. Cases outside these rules need **prior RBI Regional Office approval**. Every extension is **reported in EDPMS**.

items.title: Commission, refunds and advances: what the bank checks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Agency commission**: paid by remittance or by deduction from the invoice. The bank checks it was **declared on the EDF or SOFTEX** and accepted by customs (or, if not, why, and that a **valid agreement** exists) and that the **shipment has been made**. **Prohibited** on exports as equity in an overseas joint venture or wholly owned subsidiary, and on **Rupee Credit Route** exports except up to **10% of invoice value for tea and tobacco**.

**Refund of export proceeds**: allowed through the bank that realised them, for goods **re-imported for poor quality**, after due diligence, the bank checking that **no export incentive** was availed or it has been **surrendered**. Re-import need not be insisted on where the goods were **auctioned or destroyed** by the authorities.

**Advance from the buyer**: **ship within three years**, interest **not above the benchmark rate plus 100 basis points**, and the **documents routed through the bank that received the advance**.

items.title: Settling with neighbours: the Asian Clearing Union and the exceptions
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Asian Clearing Union (ACU)** lets member countries settle eligible payments in **ACU Dollar**, **ACU Euro** or **ACU Japanese Yen**, each equal in value to **one US dollar, euro or yen**. Banks keep these accounts with correspondents in other member countries.

Exceptions to remember:
- **Myanmar**: any freely convertible currency **in addition to** the ACU mechanism.
- **Iran** and **Sri Lanka**: eligible current account transactions, including trade, may be settled in **any permitted currency outside the ACU mechanism**.

Older books list the whole ACU group without the Sri Lanka relaxation. The Reserve Bank's current Master Direction is the authority.

items.title: Giving up on an export bill: the write-off limits and gates
items.core_explanation_md:
When an overseas buyer will not or cannot pay, an exporter can **write off** the unrealised bill, subject to limits.

**How much (a share of export proceeds realised in the preceding calendar year)**
- **Self-write-off**: **5%**, or **10%** for a **status holder**.
- **Write-off by the authorised dealer**: **10%**.
- The limits are **cumulative**.

**The gates**: outstanding for **more than a year**; **evidence of every effort** to collect; a **regular customer** for **six months** and KYC compliant; **proportionate export incentives surrendered**; a **chartered accountant's certificate** for self-write-off.

**Which cases qualify**: buyer **insolvent** (liquidator's certificate), **settled through an embassy or chamber of commerce**, goods **auctioned or destroyed** by authorities, buyer **untraceable**, an **undrawn balance** up to 10% of invoice value, legal action **out of proportion**, or a bill for a **letter-of-credit difference** that was dishonoured. For insolvency, settlement through an embassy or chamber, and goods auctioned or destroyed, the bank may write off **without limit**.

**Does not qualify**: exports to countries with **externalisation problems**, bills under **investigation** by the ED, DRI or CBI, or the subject of a **civil or criminal suit**. Write-offs are **reported in EDPMS**.

items.title: Netting a customer's exports against its imports: the set-off rules
items.core_explanation_md:
An exporter who is also an importer with the **same overseas party** may ask its bank to **set off** what it is owed against what it owes, instead of two payments crossing the world.

**Allowed**: with the **same overseas buyer/supplier**, or with **group or associate companies** through a centralised settlement arrangement.

**Conditions to check**
- **One authorised dealer** operates and supervises the arrangement.
- **No KYC, AML or CFT** concerns; transactions **not under investigation**.
- **ACU country** transactions stay **outside** it.
- **Goods against goods, services against services**: never goods against services.
- Both amounts **outstanding at the time**, and the export and import legs in the **same calendar year**.
- A **verifiable agreement** (a **written, enforceable** one for group settlement).
- **No tax avoidance**.
- Each transaction **reported separately, gross**.

The courseware adds: the **EDF is released only after the entire export proceeds have been adjusted**.

items.title: Keeping foreign exchange earned: EEFC, trade-fair and diamond accounts
items.core_explanation_md:
**EEFC account** (Exchange Earners' Foreign Currency)
- Only a **non-interest-bearing current account** with an authorised dealer.
- **100%** of foreign exchange earnings may be credited.
- Accruals in a calendar month must be **converted to rupees by the last day of the next month**, after approved uses and forward commitments.
- It is for **saving conversion costs**, not for **holding foreign currency assets**.
- **No credit**, fund-based or non-fund-based, against EEFC balances.
- A resident individual may add a **resident close relative** as joint holder (**former or survivor**).

**Trade fair account**: a **temporary** foreign currency account abroad; repatriate the balance **within one month** of the fair closing.

**Diamond Dollar Account**: for firms dealing in **diamonds and jewellery** with **three years' track record** and **average annual turnover of ₹3 crore** or more; **up to five** accounts.

items.title: Sending goods free of cost: the EDF waiver
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally every export needs an EDF. For **free-of-cost exports for export promotion**, a **status holder** can use an **EDF waiver** up to a yearly limit based on **average annual export realisation over the preceding three licensing years**:

- **2%** for most exporters.
- **Gems and jewellery, and articles of gold and precious metals**: **₹1 crore or 2%, whichever is lower**.
- **Pharmaceuticals, vaccines and life-saving drugs for health programmes of international agencies** (such as UN agencies, WHO-PAHO): up to **8%**.

Such free-of-cost supplies get **no duty drawback or other incentive**. Exports that involve **no foreign exchange transaction at all** need a **waiver from RBI**.

items.title: Export finance in two stages: before and after the ship sails
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before shipment: pre-shipment finance**
- Also called **packing credit** (PCL or EPC).
- A **working capital advance** to **buy, process or make** the goods and to pay **packing, local transport and labour**.
- The borrower normally needs a **firm export order or an export letter of credit**, and the loan is **repaid from the export proceeds**.
- Types: **export packing credit**, and **advances against government receivables** such as **duty drawback**.

**After shipment: post-shipment finance**
- Finance against the **export bills**.
- Types: bills **purchased, discounted or negotiated**; bills **sent on collection**; advances against **consignment** exports; against **undrawn balances**; against **duty drawback**.

Purpose of both: credit at **internationally comparable interest rates**, so exporters can compete.

items.title: Rupee packing credit today: the 360-day rule, not the 180-day rule
items.core_explanation_md:
Older books say a packing credit should not exceed **180 days** and may stretch to **360**. RBI's consolidated directions (Chapter XV, from November 2025) say it differently.

- **Period**: the **bank decides** it, case by case, based on the time to procure, make and ship.
- **The hard stop**: if the advance is not **adjusted by export documents within 360 days** of the advance, it **stops qualifying as export credit, from the start (ab initio)**.
- **If no export happens at all**: the bank charges the **domestic lending rate plus any penal charges** under a Board-approved policy.
- **Separate account** for each packing credit, to watch period and end-use.
- **Rate**: banks follow RBI's interest-rate directions, not the old **MCLR** rule of April 2016 in the courseware.

items.title: Paying off packing credit: bills first, flexibility for the trusted
items.core_explanation_md:
**The normal route**: the packing credit is **liquidated from the proceeds of the export bills** on purchase or discount. This **converts pre-shipment credit into post-shipment credit**.

**Other sources, by agreement**: balances in the **EEFC account**, and the exporter's **rupee resources** to the extent exports have actually taken place.

**Relaxations for good track records**
- **Substitution of contract**: liquidate from documents of **another order or commodity**, where it is **commercially necessary and unavoidable**.
- **Mark off** packing credit with proceeds of documents on which **no packing credit** was drawn, after checking **no other bank** gave packing credit for them.

**Never** for **sister, associate or group concerns**.

items.title: The running account: packing credit before the order arrives
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally a bank lends against a **firm order or letter of credit**. Where raw materials are **seasonal**, or manufacture takes longer than the delivery schedule, it may extend a **running account** and lend **before the order is in hand**.

**Who**: exporters with a **good track record**, and **EOUs and units in free trade zones, export processing zones and SEZs**. **Not sub-suppliers**.

**Conditions**
- The **order or LC must be produced within a reasonable time**.
- Export bills are marked off against the **earliest outstanding advance, first in first out**, within the **sanctioned period or 360 days**, whichever is earlier.
- **Misuse** means the facility is withdrawn at once; non-compliance means the advance is **not export credit ab initio**.

items.title: After shipment: how long, and what about the undrawn balance?
items.core_explanation_md:
**Demand bills**: credit runs for the **Normal Transit Period (NTP)**, a period fixed by **FEDAI**.

**Usance bills**: credit for **at most 365 days from the shipment date**, **including** the NTP and any grace period. The bank must **monitor the need** for the full period and **press exporters to realise early**.

**Overdue bills**: an exporter may clear overdue post-shipment credit from **rupee resources** to cut the interest cost, but the **EDF stays outstanding** and the bill is **still followed up** and reported in **EDPMS**.

**Undrawn balance**: in some trades the bill is drawn for only **90 to 98%** of FOB, the rest paid after the buyer checks quality or quantity. That balance is **contingent**, so the bank may lend against it on **commercial judgement** and the **buyer's record**.

items.title: Export credit in foreign currency: PCFC and EBR
items.core_explanation_md:
**PCFC (pre-shipment credit in foreign currency)**
- For **domestic and imported inputs**, at a rate the bank sets using a widely accepted **Alternative Reference Rate (ARR)** (LIBOR has gone).
- **Cash exports only**; any **convertible currency**, even one different from the invoice (the **cross-currency risk is the exporter's**); **ACU** exports included.
- Funded from **EEFC, RFC(D), FCNR(B)** balances, escrow accounts, overseas lines of credit, or **swaps**.
- If the exporter has **supplier's credit** for imported inputs, PCFC covers **domestic inputs only**.
- **Maximum 360 days**.

**EBR (export bills rediscounted)**
- Post-shipment credit in foreign currency, normally for **usance bills up to 180 days** from shipment, inclusive of transit and grace; longer if the borrower may draw longer usance.
- Bills rediscounted abroad **with recourse** count for export credit performance; **without recourse** do not.

items.title: The Gold Card: fewer hurdles for exporters with a good record
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who gets one**: creditworthy exporters with a **good track record**, MSMEs included, on **criteria each bank sets**. **Not** exporters on ECGC's **Specific Approval List**, or with **overdue bills above 10% of the previous year's turnover**.

**What holders get**
- **Better terms**, with interest **not above the bank's general export credit rate**.
- **Simpler, faster processing**: fresh applications in **25 days**, renewals in **15 days**, ad hoc limits in **7 days**.
- **In-principle limits for three years**, with automatic renewal.
- A **stand-by limit of at least 20% of the assessed limit** for sudden orders.
- **Relaxed inventory norms** for unanticipated orders.
- **Preference in PCFC**, lower fees, and possible **waiver of collateral** and ECGC ECIB cover.

items.title: EDPMS: one screen for every export bill
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS)** has run since **1 March 2014**. It gives authorised dealer banks **one platform** to report and monitor exports.

It **brings together** what used to be separate returns on:
- shipping bills of **caution-listed** exporters;
- **delayed use** of advances received for exports;
- exports **outstanding beyond the stipulated period**.

Banks record in it: **advance remittances** for exports, **extensions of time** for realisation, and **write-offs**. They no longer send a separate return for bills outstanding too long: the data is visible in EDPMS.

Banks also keep an **Export Bills Register**, in line with EDPMS, **numbering bills April to March**.

items.title: Chasing overdue export bills, and the caution list
items.core_explanation_md:
**The bank's duty**: watch every bill. If it is **overdue**, take it up with the exporter. If the exporter does not **deliver the proceeds or ask for an extension** in time, **report to the Reserve Bank's Regional Office**, with the reason if known.

**Documents**: the **duplicate EDF or SOFTEX** stays with the bank until **full realisation** (except for undrawn balances).

**Consequence of laxity**: seen **seriously** by RBI; **FEMA penal provisions** may be invoked.

**Caution list**: the RBI lists an exporter **on the bank's recommendation** where the exporter has come to the adverse notice of the **ED, CBI, DRI** or another agency, is **not traceable**, or is **not making sincere efforts** to realise proceeds. The bank also recommends **de-listing**. A caution-listed exporter is told of the listing and the outstanding shipping bills, and bills are accepted only on conditions.

items.title: Factoring: a service that buys the invoices and runs the ledger
items.core_explanation_md:
**What**: an ongoing arrangement where a **factor buys an exporter's book debts** from **open account** sales, **with or without recourse**, and manages credit control and the **sales ledger**.

**Three services**
1. **Debt administration**: keeps the ledger, chases payment.
2. **Credit protection**: assesses buyers' credit.
3. **Factor financing**: advances **75% to 80%** of the outstanding invoices.

**International chain**: exporter → **export factor** (finances) → **import factor** in the buyer's country (collects on the due date and remits). If the debtor does **not pay**, the import factor **steps into the export factor's shoes** to recover.

**Systems**: **single factor**; **two factor**; **direct export** factoring; **direct import** factoring.

**Why exporters use it**: immediate finance, **no letter of credit**, credit checks, ledger work done, credit protection and advice on new markets.

items.title: Forfaiting: selling a medium-term receivable for cash, with no come-back
items.core_explanation_md:
**What**: the financier **discounts** medium-term export receivables **without recourse** to the exporter, at a **fixed rate**, for the **full value**.

**Not insurance**: it is **finance**. The forfaiter judges the **importer's standing**, the **country risk**, and often relies on the **guarantee of the importer's bank**.

**The paper**: a **bill of exchange or promissory note** accepted by the importer and **guaranteed (avalised) by its bank**.

**What it costs**
- **Commitment fee**: usually **0.50% to 1.50% a year** on the unutilised part, **non-refundable**.
- **Discount charge**: a **market-related** rate for the period **plus a margin** for risk.
- **Documentation fees**.

**Benefits to the exporter**: **political and commercial risk** removed, **100% finance**, **no recourse**, no collection work, no credit insurance cost, **fixed rate**.

items.title: Factoring or forfaiting? A side-by-side
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Factoring** | **Forfaiting** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Backed by** | On-going **open account** sales, no LC | **One-off** deals backed by an **LC** or **avalised bill** |
| **Term** | **Short** | **Medium to long** (1 to 5 years) |

items.title: Paying for imports on time: the six-month rule and interest
items.core_explanation_md:
**Standard rule**: the importer should **complete remittance within six months of the date of shipment**, unless money is **withheld as a performance guarantee**.

**When payment is late**: the bank may permit settlement of dues **delayed by disputes or financial difficulties**. **Interest** on delayed payments or usance bills may be paid only for **less than three years from the shipment date**, at the **rate prescribed for trade credit**.

**Prepaying a usance bill**: the remittance is made **after deducting the interest for the unexpired part** of the usance.

items.title: Extending the time to pay an import bill: the import version of the rule
items.core_explanation_md:
An importer who cannot pay on time may ask the bank for an **extension**. The bank can grant **up to six months at a time**, to a **maximum of three years**, whatever the invoice value, if the delay is due to **disputes** about quantity or quality, **financial difficulty**, or a **suit** against the seller.

**Checks**: the invoices are **not under investigation** by the Enforcement Directorate, CBI or others; and, for an extension **beyond one year from remittance**, the importer's **total outstanding** must not exceed **USD 1 million or 10% of average import remittances over the previous two financial years, whichever is lower**.

Compare with exporters: the export test is **whichever is higher** (USD 1 million or 10% of three years' realisations). The import test is **whichever is lower**, over **two** years. **Beyond the limits**: the bank refers to the **RBI Regional Office**. Every extension is **reported in IDPMS**.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Import of Goods and Services, FED Master Direction No. 17/2016-17

items.title: Paying a supplier in advance: when a guarantee is needed
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank may allow an **advance remittance for imports without any overall ceiling**, on these conditions:

- **Up to USD 2,00,000**: no guarantee.
- **Above USD 2,00,000**: an **unconditional, irrevocable standby letter of credit** or a **guarantee** from an international bank of repute (or from an Indian bank issued against that bank's counter-guarantee).
- **Exception for private importers**: if the importer **cannot** get the guarantee and the bank is satisfied about its **track record and bona fides**, the guarantee **need not be insisted on up to USD 5 million**, under a **Board-approved policy**.
- **Public sector and government bodies**: a **specific waiver from the Ministry of Finance** is needed before remitting **more than USD 1,00,000** without a guarantee.

The bank creates an **ORM** in IDPMS for **every** such remittance.

citations.title: Master Direction - Import of Goods and Services, FED Master Direction No. 17/2016-17

items.title: When a CEO's certificate can replace the bill of entry
items.core_explanation_md:
Normally the importer shows the **exchange control copy of the bill of entry**. In place of it a bank may accept a **certificate from the CEO or auditor** that the goods have really been imported, **if both** hold:

- **less than USD 10,00,000** (one million) was remitted; and
- the importer is a **listed company with net worth of at least ₹100 crore** at its last audited balance sheet, **or** a **public sector company** or government undertaking.

The facility can also be extended to **autonomous bodies audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General**, such as scientific bodies and academic institutions. At **EDI ports** the bank downloads the bill of entry from the **BoE Master in IDPMS** and creates an **ORM**.

items.title: Financing imports, and the system that tracks them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Import letter of credit (usance)**: the importer gets **credit from the supplier** on the strength of the **bank's credibility**.

**Import loan**: a loan against **imported raw material or goods for trading**, secured by **pledge or hypothecation**; importers use them even at higher rates, waiting for prices to rise or the rupee to fall.

**Supplier's credit** vs **buyer's credit**
- **Supplier's credit**: **the overseas supplier** lends directly to the importer.
- **Buyer's credit**: the **importer arranges** a loan from a **bank or institution abroad** to pay the supplier **on immediate terms**.

**IDPMS (Import Data Processing and Monitoring System)**, in use from **10 October 2016**: customs, RBI and banks share one platform. **Customs data from the bill of entry** flows to the system and on to the bank **by its AD code**. The bank records **each step** (document submission, remittance data) **in real time**. **No separate Bill of Entry statement** is filed.

items.title: Trade credit: how long it may last
items.core_explanation_md:
Any **deferred payment arrangement** for imports, including **supplier's and buyer's credit**, is a **trade credit** if it runs for:

- up to **three years** for **capital goods**; or
- up to **one year or the operating cycle, whichever is shorter**, for **non-capital goods**.

Trade credits follow the **Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations**, not the ordinary import payment rules.

(How much a bank may approve per import, and what the **all-in cost** may be, are set in that Master Direction. Those figures have moved with the LIBOR transition and are not tested here.)

items.title: ECBs in 2026: the framework was rewritten in February
items.core_explanation_md:
Older books (and some courseware sections) describe the ECB rules of **2018-2019**: maturity of 3, 5, 7 or 10 years by end-use, an **all-in-cost cap** (benchmark plus 500 bps), an automatic route of **USD 750 million** a year, and several lender and ratio rules.

On **9 February 2026** RBI amended the Borrowing and Lending Regulations (published in the Gazette on **16 February 2026**), **before** the 30 June 2026 cut-off. The result:
- **One maturity rule** (three years) with a manufacturing carve-out.
- **No all-in-cost cap**: cost follows **market conditions**.
- A **new borrowing limit**: the higher of **USD 1 billion** or **300% of net worth**.
- A **list of end-uses that are barred**, restated in one place.

ECBs registered **before** the change continue under the old rules, except for reporting. When a question quotes the old figures, it is testing the earlier framework.

items.title: Who can borrow, from whom, in what currency
items.core_explanation_md:
**Borrower**: any resident **non-individual** incorporated, established or registered under a **Central or State Act**, **if** the governing Act allows external borrowing.
- Under a **restructuring** or **insolvency resolution**: only if the plan **specifically permits** ECB.
- With an **investigation pending** for a FEMA contravention: **allowed**, without prejudice to the outcome, but it must be **disclosed in Form ECB 1**.

**Lender**: a **person resident outside India**; a **branch abroad of an entity whose lending RBI regulates**; or a **financial institution in an IFSC**.

**Currency**: **foreign currency or rupees**; the currency can be **switched** at the rate on the date of the agreement (or a rate giving no higher liability).

**Forms**: any commercial borrowing with agreed interest and repayment, including **FCCBs and FCEBs**. Money from non-residents against **non-convertible preference shares or debentures** (after 30 April 2007) is **ECB**.

**Not ECB**: **trade credit up to three years**, **export advances**, and investments received under the **debt and non-debt instrument rules**.

items.title: How much can a company borrow abroad? The two-test limit
items.core_explanation_md:
The borrowing limit is the **higher of two tests**:

1. **Outstanding ECB** up to **USD 1 billion**; or
2. **Total outstanding borrowing** (external **and** domestic) up to **300% of net worth** (last audited standalone balance sheet).

**Counts**: the **proposed** ECB (except refinancing). **Does not count**: **non-fund-based** credit and funds from **mandatorily convertible** securities.

**Exempt from the limit**: borrowers regulated by a **financial sector regulator**.

**Route**: all ECBs that meet the Schedule's parameters can be raised under the **automatic route** (subject to reporting); everything else goes to RBI under the **approval route**.

items.title: Maturity and cost: three years, and market pricing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Minimum average maturity period (MAMP): three years.**
- **Manufacturers** may borrow with an average maturity between **one and three years**, provided such ECBs outstanding stay within **USD 150 million**.
- **Call and put options** cannot be exercised before the MAMP is complete.
- **MAMP does not have to be met** on: conversion to equity or other non-debt instruments; repayment from **non-debt instrument proceeds** received after drawdown on a repatriation basis; **refinance**; **waiver** of debt by the lender; or repayment needed for **closure, merger, demerger, liquidation** and similar actions.

**Cost of borrowing** (interest, fees, expenses, guarantee fees, export credit agency charges, but **not commitment fees or Indian statutory taxes**): **in line with market conditions**.
- Under-three-year ECBs must stay within the **trade credit cost ceiling** (and for a fixed rate loan the swap-based floating rate plus spread must not exceed it).
- **Related-party** ECBs must be at **arm's length**.

items.title: What ECB money cannot be used for
items.core_explanation_md:
Barred end-uses in India (Regulation 3A), in a mnemonic of **"chit, Nidhi, land, farm, plant, TDR, shares, old loans, on-lending"**:

- **Chit funds** and **Nidhi** companies.
- **Real estate business** and **farmhouses** (with exceptions for construction-development projects and **industrial parks** that meet the conditions).
- **Agriculture and animal husbandry**, except floriculture, horticulture and vegetables under controlled conditions, seeds, animal husbandry, aquaculture and related services.
- **Plantation**, except **tea, coffee, rubber, cardamom, palm oil and olive oil trees**.
- **Trading in TDRs**.
- **Transacting in listed or unlisted securities**, except specified **strategic corporate actions** (merger, demerger, acquisition of control and similar).
- **Repaying a domestic rupee loan** that was used for a barred purpose or is an **NPA**.
- **On-lending** for any barred purpose.

items.title: After the loan is agreed: LRN, proceeds, security, reporting
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **LRN first**: draw down only **after** the Reserve Bank gives a **Loan Registration Number** through the **designated AD Category I bank** (Form ECB 1).
2. **Proceeds**: rupee spending money must reach an **Indian rupee account** by the **end of the next month**; waiting funds may sit in an **unencumbered fixed deposit up to one year**. Foreign currency spending money may stay in a **foreign currency account** in India or abroad.
3. **Security**: charge on assets or a **guarantee** under the Guarantees Regulations 2026; the loan agreement must carry the clause; **existing lenders' no objection** for encumbered assets; **RBI-regulated entities cannot guarantee**.
4. **Reporting**: **Form ECB 2** within **seven calendar days from the end of the month** of any drawdown or servicing; **Revised Form ECB 1** within seven calendar days from the end of the month in which a change took effect. A **late submission fee** regularises delay.
5. **Untraceable** borrowers: no returns for **four consecutive quarters** and cannot be found; the bank tells **RBI and the Directorate of Enforcement**.

Also allowed: **refinancing** (without breaking the original MAMP) and **conversion into equity** with the lender's consent and no extra cost.

items.title: Trade credit for imports: amount, period, lenders
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit** is import-related credit from **outside India**. Under Schedule II of the Borrowing and Lending Regulations:

- **Amount**: up to **USD 50 million equivalent per import transaction**.
- **Period** (from the date of **shipment**): **one year, linked to the operating cycle**, for **non-capital goods**; **three years** for **capital goods**.
- **Currency**: any freely convertible currency, or **rupees**.
- **Lenders**: overseas **suppliers**, **banks and financial institutions**, **foreign equity holders**, and **IFSC** institutions.
- **Guarantees**: authorised dealers may issue **bank guarantees** in favour of the overseas supplier, bank or institution if the import and the credit comply with the norms.

Credits **up to three years** are **not ECB**: that is why trade credit sits under its own schedule.

items.title: Does the proposed ECB fit the limit?
items.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an unregulated manufacturing company has net worth of USD 600 million. It has outstanding ECB of USD 900 million and other domestic borrowings of USD 400 million, and wants to raise a further USD 200 million of ECB (a new ECB, not a refinancing). Is it within the limit?

worked_steps.description: Test (a): outstanding ECB including the proposal, against USD 1 billion.
Test (b): 300% of net worth is the ceiling on total external plus domestic borrowing.
Total borrowing after the proposal: ECB plus domestic.
The limit is the higher of the two tests, so the borrower may use whichever it passes.

items.final_answer_with_unit: The proposal fits: it fails the USD 1 billion test but passes the 300%-of-net-worth test (USD 1,500 million against USD 1,800 million), and the limit is the higher of the two

self_check.expected_takeaway: USD 1,400 million: 1,800 less 400 of domestic borrowing, which means a further USD 500 million on top of the USD 900 million outstanding.

items.title: The investee company's forms: who files what, and when
items.core_explanation_md:
**The company that receives foreign money files** (under the Mode of Payment and Reporting Regulations):

| Form | What it reports | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FC-GPR** | Issue of equity to a non-resident that counts as **FDI** | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **ESOP** | Stock options to non-resident employees or directors | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **LLP (I)** | An LLP receiving capital contribution or profit share consideration | **Within 30 days** of receiving the money |
| **CN** | A start-up issuing **convertible notes** to a non-resident | **Within 30 days** of issue |
| **InVI** | An **investment vehicle** issuing units to a non-resident | **Within 30 days** of the issue |
| **FLA** | **Annual** return of foreign liabilities and assets, by a company that received FDI or an LLP that received capital contribution | By **15 July** each year (the year runs April to March) |

items.title: Transfers of shares between residents and non-residents: Form FC-TRS and LLP (II)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Form FC-TRS** is filed when equity instruments move
- between a **non-resident holding on a repatriable basis** and a **non-resident holding on a non-repatriable basis**, or
- between a **non-resident holding on a repatriable basis** and a **resident**.

**Who files**: the **resident** transferor or transferee, or the **non-resident holding on a non-repatriable basis**. A non-resident who **sells on a recognised stock exchange** reports it **himself**.

**When**: within **60 days** of the transfer or of the **receipt or remittance of funds, whichever is earlier**. For **deferred payment**, report on receipt of **each tranche**.

**Not reported**: a **sale** between a non-resident holding on a **non-repatriable** basis and a **resident**.

**LLPs**: disinvestment or transfer of capital or profit share between a resident and a non-resident is reported in **Form LLP (II)** within **60 days** of receipt of funds, with the onus on the **resident**.

items.title: What the banks and investing companies report
items.core_explanation_md:
**Banks** (authorised dealers) report **purchases by foreign investors on Indian stock exchanges**:
- **Form LEC (FII)**: purchases or transfers by **foreign portfolio investors**.
- **Form LEC (IFI)**: purchases or transfers by an **individual resident outside India**, including **NRIs and OCIs**.

**Downstream investment** (an Indian company that has foreign investment investing in another Indian entity, where it counts as **indirect foreign investment** for the investee):
- **notify the Secretariat for Industrial Assistance, DPIIT** within **30 days** of the investment, and
- file **Form DI** with the Reserve Bank within **30 days** of allotment.

One useful way to remember the timings: **30 days to report an issue or an allotment; 60 days to report a transfer; 15 July for the annual return.**

items.title: FEDAI Rule 1: when the dealing day runs, and what a known holiday is
items.core_explanation_md:
**FEDAI** is the dealers' association whose rules govern how authorised dealers handle forex. Its **Rule 1** deals with time.

- **Normal market hours**: **9.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m. IST** on working days, for inter-bank and client transactions in on-shore deliverable foreign currency/rupee deals, **as prescribed by the RBI** for inter-bank transactions (older books show a **4.30 p.m. customer cut-off**, now gone).
- **Beyond hours**: allowed on **business days** for customers and banks, **provided the NOOP limit** (net overnight open position) is **maintained at all times**, including from end of day to 9 a.m. next day.
- **Individuals** (including joint accounts and proprietary firms): may deal **even on Saturdays, Sundays and holidays**, under the bank's policy.
- **Spot date rolls over at 12.00 midnight IST.**
- **Saturday** is not a working business day for forex, except for those individual deals.
- **Known holiday**: known **at least three working business days** before the date. Any other holiday is **suddenly declared**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 2: pricing and recovering an export bill
items.core_explanation_md:
**Buying the bill**: at the bank's **current bill buying rate** or the **contracted rate**. **Interest** for the **transit period and/or usance** is taken **up front**.

**If the bill is not paid on time**: each bank has its **own, published crystallisation policy**. On crystallisation the bank applies its **TT selling rate**; the customer owes the **crystallised rupee amount plus interest and charges**, and interest runs **from the crystallisation date** until recovery. Bills for **countries with externalisation problems** are crystallised under the same policy, even if payment was made in **local currency**.

**If the proceeds arrive after crystallisation**: converted at the **TT buying rate** (or the contract rate).

**If the bill is dishonoured before crystallisation**: the bank recovers the **rupee equivalent and foreign currency charges at the TT selling rate**, with interest and rupee charges.

**Paid early**: **interest for the unexpired period is refunded**, and **notional swap cost** is paid or recovered.

items.title: Normal transit period: the number of days, by type of bill
items.core_explanation_md:
The **normal transit period (NTP)** is the **average time from negotiation or discount until the money arrives**. It is **not** the time the goods take to reach the buyer.

- **Fixed due date** (usance bills reckoned from shipment or bill date): **no NTP**.
- **DP or sight bills, not under LC**: **foreign currency 25 days; rupee 20 days**.
- **Rupee bills under LC**: **3 days** (reimbursement at the negotiating centre), **7 days** (elsewhere in India), **20 days** (banks outside India, or RBI under state credit).
- **TT reimbursement under LC**: **5 days** where by electronic means; **5 days plus the extra period** where the LC says the claim comes later.
- **UN guideline countries**: **maximum 120 days**.
- A bank may use a **different NTP** for exceptional cases with **documented reasons**; finance **beyond the prescribed NTP** is capped at **90 days from shipment**; **no change in due date** after purchase, discount or negotiation.

items.title: Rules 2.4, 2.5 and 4: collections, tenor changes, remittances and delays
items.core_explanation_md:
**Export bills on collection or consignment**: proceeds are converted at the **TT buying rate** (or contract rate) **only after the money is credited to the bank's Nostro account**. The bank must credit the exporter **within two working business days**; if late, it pays **compensation at the minimum export credit rate** plus compensation for **adverse exchange movement**.

**Remittances**: **outward** at the **TT selling rate**; **inward** at the **TT buying rate** (or contract rate). The bank must inform or pay the beneficiary **within two working business days** of the credit advice. If late, it pays **interest at 2% over its savings rate**. If the beneficiary says nothing for **five working business days** and the bank does not return the money, it must **crystallise the remittance** within the time allowed for surrendering foreign currency.

**Vostro transfers between banks (Rule 4.6)**: the remitting bank sends **Form A3 within five working business days**; beyond that it pays **₹1,000 a day**; a claim lodged after **15 days** is capped at **₹10,000**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 3: import bills
items.core_explanation_md:
**Retiring or crystallising an import bill**: at the **hedge contract rate** if the importer has a hedge; otherwise at the **prevailing bill selling rate**.

**Unpaid foreign currency import bills under letters of credit** are **crystallised under the bank's stated policy**.

**Interest**: bills negotiated under import letters of credit carry the **commercial rate for the bank's domestic advances**; interest on **interest-bearing bills** follows **RBI's directive**.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 5: contracts, delivery dates and quotes
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Definite amounts and periods**.
- **Delivery**: **ready or cash** = **same day**; **value next day** = the **next working business day**; **spot** = the **second working business day** after the deal; **forward** = beyond spot, with the period counted from the **spot value date**.
- **Option period** chosen by the customer: **not beyond one month**; the contract states the **first and last dates**.
- **Holidays**: if the fixed date or last option date is a **known holiday**, the last delivery date is the **preceding** working business day; if it is a **suddenly declared holiday**, the **next** working business day.
- **Date of delivery**: bills **negotiated, purchased or discounted** = the date of **negotiation and payment of rupees**; bills **on collection** = the date **rupees are paid on realisation**; **import bills** = **retirement or crystallisation, whichever is earlier**.
- **Merchant has the option of delivery** (except NDDC).
- **Quotes** in **direct terms** (rupees and paise per 1 or 100 units); **rounding** to the rupee or actual paise under the bank's policy.

items.title: FEDAI Rule 6: early delivery, extension and cancellation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Optional for the bank**: accepting or giving **early delivery**, or **extending** a contract. The **customer must deliver or ask** for extension or cancellation **on or before maturity**.

- **Early delivery**: the bank recovers or pays the **swap difference**, plus **interest on the funds outlay or inflow**; **swap cost is recovered from the customer** even if no swap is actually done.
- **Extension** = **cancel** at the appropriate rate on that date and **rebook at the current rate**; the **cancellation difference** is settled.
- **Cancellation** at the customer's request: the customer pays or receives the **difference between the contract rate and the cancellation rate**. **Purchase contracts** cancel at the **TT selling rate**; **sale contracts** at the **TT buying rate** (the **forward** TT rate if before maturity).
- **Recovery** may be a **lump sum or instalments**, uniformly over the **remaining maturity**, at least **quarterly**, never beyond maturity, under a **Board-approved policy**.
- **A contract that becomes impossible to perform is not void**: the customer must apply for cancellation.
- **No instructions after maturity**: the bank **cancels within three working business days**; the customer **bears any loss** but **gets no gain**, unless the delay was **beyond the client's control** and the bank records why.

items.title: FEDAI Rules 7 and 8: brokers and settling between banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rule 7: intermediaries**
- FEDAI accredits **exchange brokers (voice)** only. **Electronic platforms** (multi-bank portals, order matching systems) need **RBI authorisation**.
- Banks use only **accredited** intermediaries, and pay **no brokerage or fees to other bank employees**.
- Every contract, confirmation and advice carries **"Subject to the Rules & Regulations of the Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India"**; **no contract with an intermediary as principal**.

**Rule 8: delays between banks**
- A **seller bank** that delivers funds late pays **interest for the days of delay at 2% over the overnight benchmark** of the currency.
- The buyer bank must accept **back-valued** funds delivered **within two working business days** of the due date; later, it may choose **value-dated funds or interest**.
- **Claim within 15 working business days** of the due date, or interest is **capped at 60 days**; the seller bank must **settle within 15 working business days** of the claim, or pay interest for the **whole** period.
- **60 days** unsettled: refer to **FEDAI**, whose decision binds both banks.
- Banks dealing in forex forwards must be members of **CCIL's forex forward guaranteed settlement** segment.

items.title: What the Act means by foreign exchange, and by capital and current account
items.core_explanation_md:
The statute gives precise definitions.

**Foreign currency** = **any currency other than Indian currency**.

**Foreign exchange** = foreign currency **and**:
1. **deposits, credits and balances payable in any foreign currency**;
2. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange expressed or drawn in Indian currency but payable in foreign currency**;
3. **drafts, travellers cheques, letters of credit or bills of exchange drawn by banks, institutions or persons outside India but payable in Indian currency**.

**Capital account transaction**: one that **alters the assets or liabilities**, including contingent liabilities, **outside India of residents**, or **in India of non-residents**.

**Current account transaction**: **any other**, including payments for **foreign trade**, other current business and services, **short-term banking and credit facilities** in the ordinary course; **interest on loans and net investment income**; **remittances for living expenses** of parents, spouse and children abroad; and **foreign travel, education and medical care** of parents, spouse and children.

items.title: Sections 10 to 12: what an authorised person must do, and what RBI can do
items.core_explanation_md:
**Authorisation (s.10)**: the Reserve Bank **authorises** authorised dealers, money changers and offshore banking units, and may **revoke** the authorisation in the **public interest** or for **non-compliance** (after giving a **reasonable chance to represent**).

**Declaration (s.10(5))**: **before any transaction** the authorised person must **ask for a declaration and information** that reasonably satisfy it the transaction is **not designed to contravene or evade** the Act. If the customer **refuses** or complies **unsatisfactorily**, it must **refuse in writing**, and **report to the Reserve Bank** if it thinks a contravention is planned.

**Misuse of purchased exchange (s.10(6))**: a customer who buys foreign exchange for a declared purpose and **does not use it for that purpose**, **does not surrender it in time**, or uses it for a **non-permissible** purpose is **deemed to have contravened** the Act.

**Directions (s.11)**: RBI can direct authorised persons and require information; **contravening a direction or failing to file a return** can cost up to **₹10,000** plus up to **₹2,000 a day** if continuing.

**Inspection (s.12)**: RBI may inspect an authorised person's business.

items.title: Section 13: the penalty arithmetic
items.core_explanation_md:
Anyone who **contravenes the Act, a rule, regulation, notification, direction or order, or a condition of an authorisation**, is liable **on adjudication** to:

- **up to three times the sum involved**, where the amount is **quantifiable**; or
- **up to ₹2 lakh**, where it is **not quantifiable**; and
- if the contravention **continues**, a **further penalty of up to ₹5,000 for every day after the first day**.

**Foreign assets above the prescribed threshold** (s.13(1A)): up to **three times the sum involved** and **confiscation of equivalent value in India**.

A way to remember: **3 times, ₹2 lakh, ₹5,000 a day after day one**.

items.title: The dealing room: keeping dealers, books and records apart
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI's Internal Control Guidelines rest on **one principle**: **separate the people who deal from the people who record, check and settle**.

- **Front office**: the **dealing room**.
- **Mid-office**: **risk management**, accounting policies and management information.
- **Back office**: **settlement, reconciliation and accounting**.

**Controls on dealers**
- **No accounting work** for dealers.
- **Deal slips** with broker, counterparty, currencies, amounts, **time**, rate and due dates, passed **without delay** to the back office.
- The **system stamps** the trading date, time and serial number; a dealer **cannot alter** them without authorisation. **Late deals** are marked and sent to an official **unconnected with the dealer**.
- **Voice recording**, tapes kept **at least two months** (longer if there is a dispute).
- An **annual break of two weeks or longer** for every dealer.
- Written acceptance of the **FEDAI and FIMMDA codes of conduct**.

citations.title: Internal Control Guidelines (3 February 2011)

items.title: The back office and the brokers: confirmations, panels and brokerage
items.core_explanation_md:
**Back office**
- **Independent confirmation** of contracts (except deals through **CCIL**); **dealers never sign confirmations**.
- Discrepancies **rectified the same day**; **no backlog**.
- **Rate-scan reports** at least **three times a day** where the system lacks the facility; deals at wide variance from market are questioned.

**Exchange brokers**
- **Cannot act as principals** or hold positions.
- **Broker's notes** received **before close of business** on the deal day and **reconciled the same day**.
- **No nominating** a broker for a deal not put through the broker.
- A panel of ideally **five or six** brokers, **reviewed annually**.
- **Dealing staff play no part** in scrutinising or paying **brokerage claims**; a **monthly broker-wise statement** goes to management.
- Brokers' malpractice goes to **FEDAI**.
- **Substituting** one bank for another in an inter-bank contract through a broker is **prohibited**.

items.title: Risks in forex dealing and how limits and documents contain them
items.core_explanation_md:
**Five risks**
1. **Credit**: **pre-settlement** (the **replacement cost** if the counterparty defaults before the deal settles) and **settlement** (paying **before** the counterparty does).
2. **Liquidity**: unable to fund or to **exit a position at a fair price**.
3. **Gap / interest rate**: moves in interest-rate differentials.
4. **Legal**: handled by **master agreements** (**ISDA, IFEMA, ICOM**).
5. **Operational**: systems and a **written contingency plan**.

**Limits**: set **globally** for local inter-bank and overseas business; **every dealer is told his limit**; deals are **counted against limits** and **aggregated at close of business**; **excesses are reported and approved**; **breaches of regulatory limits go to RBI**.

**Documents**: forwards up to **13 months** with customers need a **stamped contract note**; inter-bank, **unsigned computer confirmations plus a one-time stamped indemnity**. **Beyond 13 months** and for other derivatives, an **ISDA Master Agreement** with signed confirmations. Corporate clients give a **Board resolution** authorising their dealers.

items.title: Nostro reconciliation, Vostro monitoring and audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Nostro reconciliation** (RBI calls it an **essential control**)
- **Statements at least weekly**, reconciled against the **mirror account** on the **same date**.
- Put routine items such as **export bills purchased** and **drafts issued** through **suspense accounts** to reduce unreconciled items.
- **No set-off** of debit and credit items and **no write-off** of unreconciled items to profit and loss except as RBI allows.
- A **monthly report** with **large** and **age-wise** unreconciled items.

**Vostro monitoring**: watch funds flow, **concealed overdrafts**, sudden changes in activity; assess correspondent banks' credit risk **at least once in twelve months**; get **balance confirmations**.

**Audit**: internal audit reviews limit excesses; a **special audit of the dealing room and its systems at least once a year**; **concurrent audit** is part of the **early warning system**.

items.title: The two forex exposure limits and how the net open position is counted
items.core_explanation_md:
**Net Overnight Open Position Limit (NOOPL)**: fixed by the **Board**, told to RBI, **not above 25% of total capital (Tier I and Tier II)**. It drives the **capital charge** on forex risk. A second limit for **rupee positions** (**NOP-INR**) may be prescribed by RBI.

**Counting the position**
1. For each currency add the **net spot**, **net forward** and **net options (delta-equivalent)** positions.
2. Convert each currency's and gold's net position into **rupees**.
3. Add all the **net short** positions, and separately all the **net long** positions.
4. The overall net position is the **higher** of the two sums (the **shorthand method**).
5. **Offshore** positions are worked out **separately** and **never netted** with onshore ones.

**Aggregate Gap Limit (AGL)**: set by the **Board**, **not above six times total capital**. Banks with **tenor-wise PV01 and VaR limits** may use those instead.

The **ALCO or an internal audit committee** monitors adherence.

items.title: FDI, FPI and foreign investment: the ten per cent line
items.core_explanation_md:
Everything in foreign investment starts from **one test: how much of a company does the non-resident hold, and is it listed?**

- **FDI**: investment in **equity instruments** by a person resident outside India in
  - an **unlisted** Indian company (any amount), or
  - **10% or more** of the **post-issue paid-up equity capital, on a fully diluted basis**, of a **listed** company.
- **FPI (portfolio investment)**: **less than 10%** of a **listed** company's equity on a fully diluted basis.
- **Once FDI, always FDI**: if a holding in a listed company **falls below 10%**, it **still counts as FDI**.
- **Fully diluted** means all shares that would be outstanding **if every conversion right were exercised**.
- **Foreign investment** is the umbrella: investment on a **repatriable basis** in equity instruments of an Indian company or the capital of an **LLP**. One investor may hold **either FDI or FPI in a given company**.
- An **FPI** (the investor) is a person **registered with SEBI** under the FPI Regulations, 2014.

items.title: What counts as an equity instrument, and the 25% rule on part-paid shares and warrants
items.core_explanation_md:
**Equity instruments** = **equity shares**, **convertible debentures**, **preference shares** and **share warrants** issued by an Indian company.

- **Equity shares** include **partly paid** shares.
- **Convertible debentures** and **preference shares** count only if **fully and mandatorily convertible** and **fully paid**.
- **Partly paid shares** issued to a non-resident: **25% of the total consideration (premium included) upfront** and the shares **fully called up within 12 months**.
- **Share warrants**: **at least 25% upfront**, the **balance within 18 months**.
- An **optionality clause** is allowed only with a **minimum lock-in of one year** (or the sector's period, whichever is higher) and **no assured-price exit**.

items.title: Sectors closed to foreign direct investment
items.core_explanation_md:
**No FDI** in:

1. **Lottery** business (government, private, online).
2. **Gambling and betting**, including **casinos**.
3. **Chit funds**.
4. **Nidhi companies**.
5. **Trading in transferable development rights (TDR)**.
6. **Real estate business** or **construction of farm houses**. (Real estate business means dealing in land and property **to earn profit**; it **excludes** townships, residential or commercial premises, roads, bridges, educational and recreational facilities, city-level infrastructure, **broking**, **REITs** and **rental income**.)
7. **Manufacture of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes** of tobacco or tobacco substitutes.
8. Activities **not open to private investment**, such as **atomic energy** and **railway operations** (except permitted activities).

items.title: Downstream investment: foreign money passed on through an Indian company
items.core_explanation_md:
When an **Indian entity that has received indirect foreign investment** (one that is **owned or controlled by non-residents**) invests in **another Indian company**, the investee is treated as having **indirect foreign investment**, and must meet the **entry route, sectoral cap, pricing guidelines and conditions** that apply to foreign investment.

**Conditions on the investing entity**
- **Board approval** (and any shareholders' agreement).
- **Bring funds from abroad**; do **not** use funds **borrowed in the domestic market**. **Internal accruals** (profits moved to reserves **after tax**) are fine.

**Counting rules**
- Shares a non-resident gets by **converting debt** are **counted** as foreign investment.
- **FCCBs and DRs with debt underlying** are **not** counted.

items.title: Individuals abroad buying listed shares: the 10% and 24% limits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who**: since **12 June 2026**, **any individual resident outside India**, not only NRIs and OCIs (RBI operationalised it on **15 June 2026**).

**How**: buy and sell on a **recognised stock exchange**, through a **branch designated by an authorised dealer**.

**Limits**
- **One individual**: **less than 10%** of the company's paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis. Holdings under **Schedules II, III and any other schedule** are **added** for this test.
- **All such individuals together**: **not more than 24%**.

**If the 10% limit is breached**: **divest within five trading days** of the settlement date of the trades that caused it. The designated branch tells the **depositories and the company within seven trading days**. If the person does **not** divest, the **whole investment becomes FDI** and **no further portfolio investment** is allowed in that company.

**NRIs and OCIs may also, without limit**: buy or sell **domestic mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**, buy **shares of public sector enterprises being disinvested by the Government**, and subscribe to the **National Pension System**.

items.title: NRIs investing on a non-repatriation basis: what is open and what is closed
items.core_explanation_md:
**Open, without any limit** (on or off the exchange): **equity instruments** of Indian companies, **units of investment vehicles**, **capital of an LLP**, **convertible notes of startups**, and **mutual fund units** investing **more than 50% in equity**. Such investment is treated as **domestic investment**, at par with residents.

**Closed**: no investment under this route in a **Nidhi company**, or a company in **agriculture or plantation**, **real estate business**, **farm house construction** or **TDRs**.

**Firms and proprietary concerns**: an NRI or OCI may put capital into a firm or proprietary concern on a non-repatriation basis if it is **not** in **agriculture or plantation**, **print media** or **real estate business**.

items.title: Sending sale proceeds and NRO balances abroad: USD 1 million, undertakings and the property cap
items.core_explanation_md:
**NRIs and PIOs** may remit up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (including transfers to **NRE** and **SNRR** accounts) out of **NRO balances**, **sale proceeds of assets** and **assets inherited**, on documentary evidence, through **one authorised dealer** if paid in instalments.

items.title: Exports that need no declaration form
items.core_explanation_md:
The declaration form (EDF) is the exporter's statement to the bank and customs of what is leaving. **Regulation 4** lists cases where **no declaration is needed**:

- **Trade samples** and **publicity material** supplied **free**.
- **Personal effects** of travellers.
- **Ship's stores**, **trans-shipment cargo** and goods supplied to **Government or defence** orders.
- **Gifts** with an exporter's declaration that the value is **not more than ₹5 lakh**.
- **Aircraft and engines** sent abroad for overhaul or repair and **re-imported within six months**.
- Goods **imported free on a re-export basis**; goods sent abroad **for testing** (to be re-imported); **replacement goods** exported free under the Foreign Trade Policy.
- **Defective goods sent for repair and re-import**, with an **authorised dealer's certificate that no foreign exchange is involved**.
- Re-export of **defective, loaned or surplus imported goods** that a **Development Commissioner** (SEZ, technology park, free trade zone) permits.
- Exports **the Reserve Bank permits** on application.

**Important**: no form does **not** mean no obligation: the exporter must still **realise and repatriate** the proceeds.

citations.locator: Regulation 4(a) to (k); Master Direction on Export of Goods and Services, paragraph B.12

items.title: Waiver of the declaration form and the status holder free-of-cost limit
items.core_explanation_md:
Where **no foreign exchange is involved at all**, the **Reserve Bank** must waive the declaration procedure. An **authorised dealer** may, however, **waive the form** for **status holder** exporters who send **freely exportable goods free of cost** to promote exports, within a yearly cap:

| Exporter | Annual cap on free-of-cost exports |
| --- | --- |
| Most exporters | **2%** of the **average annual export realisation of the last three licensing years** |
| Gems and jewellery; gold and precious metals articles | the **lower of ₹1 crore and 2%** |
| Supplies of **vaccines, drugs, pharmaceuticals** to UN, WHO-PAHO or Government **health programmes** | up to **8%** |

Such free supplies get **no duty drawback or other export incentive**.

citations.title: Master Direction - Export of Goods and Services

items.title: Trade in rupees: invoicing and settlement through the Special Rupee Vostro Account
items.core_explanation_md:
Exports and imports may be **invoiced, paid and settled in rupees**, as an **additional** route beside foreign currency and the Asian Clearing Union.

**How the money moves**
- An **authorised dealer in India** opens a **Special Rupee Vostro Account (SRVA)** for a **bank resident outside India** (or a branch of an Indian bank abroad).
- **Importer in India** pays **rupees** into the partner bank's SRVA against the supplier's invoice.
- **Exporter in India** is paid **rupees out of the balance** in the SRVA.
- The SRVA can be funded by **inward remittances** or transfers from other **repatriable rupee accounts**.
- The dealer may open an **additional current account** exclusively for settling trade.
- **FEDAI** publishes a **directory of SRVAs**.

**Limit of this card**: the Master Direction's own paragraph on rupee trade settlement was **rewritten on 17 July 2026**, after the cut-off date used for this course. The account mechanics above are the stable part.

items.title: eBRC and closing small export entries by declaration
items.core_explanation_md:
The **export monitoring system (EDPMS)** records each export and its realisation.

- Banks update it **as and when proceeds are realised**.
- The **electronic bank realisation certificate (eBRC)** is generated **only from EDPMS data** (since **16 October 2017**), so the two always agree.

**Small entries: ₹10 lakh or less per entry or bill**
- The bank **reconciles and closes** them on the **exporter's declaration** that the money has been realised.
- A **reduction in declared or invoice value** is also accepted on the exporter's declaration.
- Declarations may be taken **quarterly**, covering **several bills together**.
- The bank **reviews its charges** on such small transactions and levies **no penalty** for delay in following regulatory guidelines.

Above ₹10 lakh the usual proof of realisation applies.

items.title: Forfaiting and non-recourse export factoring
items.core_explanation_md:
**Forfaiting**: **EXIM Bank and authorised dealers** may **buy export receivables without recourse to the exporter**; commitment fees and service charges may be paid **in advance as a lump sum or monthly**.

**Export factoring on a non-recourse basis**
- A bank decides **for itself** whether to factor; it must **not over-finance** the client and the invoices must be **genuine trade invoices**.
- The **export factor** needs an arrangement with an **import factor** abroad for **credit evaluation and collection**.
- The invoice carries a **notation that the importer pays the import factor**.
- After factoring, the export factor may **close the export bills** and report in **EDPMS**.
- With **no import factor**, the export factor may take credit information from the **correspondent bank abroad**.
- The export factor does **KYC and due diligence on the exporter**.

citations.title: Master Direction - Export of Goods and Services

items.title: Advance remittance for imports and the time to settle import dues
items.core_explanation_md:
**Advance remittance for goods**: no ceiling, but:

| Advance | What the bank needs |
| --- | --- |
| **Up to USD 200,000** | no guarantee |
| **Above USD 200,000** | an **unconditional irrevocable standby L/C or guarantee** from an **international bank of repute** (or an Indian AD's guarantee against that bank's counter-guarantee) |
| Private importer **unable to get a guarantee** | dealer may waive up to **USD 5 million**, if satisfied on **track record**, under a **Board-approved policy** |
| **PSU/Government** unable to get one | **Ministry of Finance waiver** for an advance **above USD 100,000** |

**Time limits**: remit import payments within **six months** of shipment. A dealer may **extend by six months at a time, up to three years**; to go **beyond one year from the date of remittance**, the importer's **total outstanding** must be within the **lower of USD 1 million and 10% of the average import remittances of the previous two financial years**.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Import of Goods and Services

items.title: IDPMS: the outward remittance message and the bill of entry
items.core_explanation_md:
The **import monitoring system (IDPMS)** matches **money out** with **goods in**.

- On each **advance remittance** the bank creates an **Outward Remittance Message (ORM)**.
- The **bill of entry**: for **electronic ports** the bank **downloads it from the BoE master** using the importer's AD code; for other ports the bank **uploads** the data.
- The bill of entry is then **marked against the ORM**, closing the loop.
- An **extension of time** is reported as a **"Bill of Entry Extension"**, with the **extension date** entered.

If goods have not come in, the bank follows up and, where the supplier fails to deliver, the advance must be **brought back**.

citations.authority: Reserve Bank of India
citations.title: Master Direction - Import of Goods and Services

items.title: Trade credit: supplier's credit, buyer's credit and the ceilings
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit** = credit from an **overseas supplier, bank or institution** to pay for **permissible imports**.

- **Supplier's credit**: given by the **overseas supplier**.
- **Buyer's credit**: a **loan the importer arranges from an overseas bank** to pay the supplier.

| Feature | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Amount | up to **USD 50 million per import transaction** |
| Period (from **date of shipment**) | **non-capital goods**: up to **one year** (linked to the operating cycle); **capital goods**: up to **three years** |
| Currency | any **freely convertible currency** or **rupees** |
| Cost (foreign currency) | **not more than 250 bp over the 6-month benchmark** |
| Cost (rupee) | **market-linked** |
| Lenders | overseas suppliers, banks, financial institutions, **foreign equity holders**, **IFSC** institutions |

Trade credit of **original maturity up to three years is not ECB**.

items.title: Drawing down an ECB: the loan number and where the money goes
items.core_explanation_md:
**Before any money comes in**: the borrower gets a **Loan Registration Number (LRN)** from the **Reserve Bank**, through its **designated AD Category I bank** (the bank it has chosen to report and monitor the loan). **No LRN, no drawdown.**

**Where the proceeds land**
- For a **permitted rupee spend in India**: credit them to a **rupee account with the designated bank** by the **end of the next month**. Until used, they may be held in an **unencumbered fixed deposit of up to one year** with that bank.
- For a **permitted foreign currency spend**: a **foreign currency account** with the designated bank in India, **or** one **outside India**.

items.title: The ECB forms and their deadlines
items.core_explanation_md:
| Form | Reports | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ECB 1** | the loan's details, to **obtain the LRN** | **before drawdown** |
| **Revised ECB 1** | **any change** in what was reported | **within 7 calendar days from the end of the month** in which the change took effect |
| **ECB 2** | **receipt of proceeds** and **debt servicing**; any event that **changes the outstanding** | **within 7 calendar days from the end of the month** of the receipt or servicing |

**Late?** Finish the report, then pay the **late submission fee**.

**LRN cancelled** only on the borrower's request and only if **no drawdown** has occurred.

**Untraceable borrower**: an active LRN holder who files **no return for four consecutive quarters**, where the bank has **documented repeated failed attempts** to reach the borrower, its **auditors, directors or promoters**, and finds it **not operating at its registered office**.

items.title: Turning an ECB into shares
items.core_explanation_md:
An ECB, **even one that has matured but not been paid**, can be **converted into a non-debt instrument** (for example equity), under the **Non-Debt Instruments Rules**.

**Conditions**
- **No extra cost** to the lender for enabling the conversion.
- The **lender consents**.
- **Other lenders** consent, or are at least **informed**.
- If the borrower also borrows from an **RBI-regulated entity**, **prudential rules (including restructuring)** apply.

**How much converts**: the liability is fixed at the **exchange rate on the date of the conversion agreement**, or any rate that gives a figure **no higher** than that.

**Minimum average maturity (MAMP) need not be met** for: conversion to non-debt instruments; repayment from **repatriable equity proceeds received after the drawdown**; **refinance**; **waiver of debt by the lender**; repayment required for **corporate actions** such as merger, demerger or liquidation.

**Cash limit**: for most destinations a traveller may buy **notes and coins only up to USD 3,000 per visit**. The rest travels as a **stored value card, travellers cheque or bank draft**.

items.title: Coming home: surrender, what you may bring in and cards abroad
items.core_explanation_md:
**On return**
- **Surrender unspent notes and travellers cheques within 180 days**, but you may **keep up to USD 2,000** (or credit it to an **RFC (Domestic)** account).
- **Foreign coins**: hold **without limit**.
- A resident back from a temporary visit may bring in **Indian notes up to ₹25,000** (Nepal and Bhutan have their own rules).
- **Anyone arriving**: bring foreign exchange **without limit**, but **declare it to customs** on the **Currency Declaration Form** if **notes, bank notes and travellers cheques together exceed USD 10,000**, or **currency notes alone exceed USD 5,000**.

**Cards abroad**
- **International debit cards** from an authorised dealer: cash or shop payments abroad, **within the LRS limit**, **permissible current account items only**.
- **International credit cards from overseas issuers**: allowed for residents with a **foreign currency account**; pay from that account or by remittance **direct to the card issuer** through the holder's own bank. **No RBI ceiling** on this facility.
- **Never** for **prohibited items** (such as lottery tickets); **not usable in Nepal and Bhutan**.

items.title: Overseas direct investment: what counts and what stays counted
items.core_explanation_md:
**ODI** is an **Indian resident's investment in a foreign entity** that is any of:

1. **Unlisted equity capital** of a foreign entity.
2. **Subscription to the memorandum** of a foreign entity.
3. **10% or more** of the paid-up equity of a **listed** foreign entity.
4. **Less than 10% but with control** of a listed foreign entity.

**Once ODI, always ODI**: it stays ODI even if the holding **drops below 10%** or **control is lost**.

**Financial commitment** = ODI + **debt** (other than portfolio investment) in the foreign entity, **plus non-fund-based facilities** given to or for it.

**Foreign entity** = a body formed **outside India** (an **IFSC** counts) with **limited liability**. The limited liability condition is **waived** if its core activity is in a **strategic sector**.

items.title: Overseas investment: the 400% ceiling and the closed activities
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ceiling for an Indian entity**: total **financial commitment in all foreign entities together** must not exceed **400% of net worth** at the **last audited balance sheet** (or as RBI directs).

- **Not counted**: capitalisation of **retained earnings**.
- **Counted**: use of money raised through **ADRs/GDRs**; use of **ECB proceeds** (to the extent the pledge or charge on assets for them has not already been counted).
- **Outside the limit**: **Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna** PSUs and their subsidiaries in **strategic sectors**.
- **Overseas portfolio investment** by an Indian entity: up to **50% of net worth**.

**ODI is barred in**
- **real estate activity** (buying and selling property or **TDR trading**; building townships, premises, roads or bridges for **sale or lease** is not "real estate activity");
- **gambling** in any form;
- **financial products linked to the rupee**, unless the **Reserve Bank** specifically approves.

**Start-ups abroad**: an Indian entity may invest only from **internal accruals** of itself or its Indian group or associates; a resident **individual** only from **own funds**.

items.title: Guarantees and the exchange control line: who may be a party
items.core_explanation_md:
A **guarantee** (including a **counter-guarantee**) is a contract to **perform a promise or pay a debt if the principal debtor defaults**. Three roles:

- **Creditor**: the person who **receives** the guarantee.
- **Principal debtor**: the person whose **default** is covered.
- **Surety**: the person who **gives** it.

**The rule**: a **resident of India** may be a party (debtor, surety or creditor) to a guarantee **with a non-resident party only as these regulations allow**, or with the Reserve Bank's permission.

**Not covered by the regulations**
- A guarantee given by an **authorised dealer's branch outside India or in an IFSC** (unless another party is resident in India).
- An **Irrevocable Payment Commitment** by an authorised dealer as **custodian bank**, where the debtor is a **registered FPI** and the creditor an **authorised central counterparty**.
- A guarantee given under the **Overseas Investment Regulations, 2022**.

**Link to standby credits**: a **standby letter of credit** works like a guarantee (the seller claims by declaring the customer defaulted), so an authorised dealer's standby that backs an exposure between a resident and a non-resident is dealt with under this guarantee framework.

items.title: Who may be surety, debtor or creditor, and the two tests
items.core_explanation_md:
**A resident acting as surety or principal debtor** must satisfy **both**:
1. The **underlying transaction is not prohibited** under FEMA.
2. The **surety and the principal debtor are eligible to lend to and borrow from each other** under the **Borrowing and Lending Regulations, 2018**.

**Test 2 is waived** for:
- a guarantee by an **authorised dealer bank** that is **covered by a counter-guarantee**, or issued against **100% collateral in a deposit**, from a **non-resident**;
- a guarantee by the **India agent of a foreign shipping or airline company** for its liability to a **statutory or Government authority** in India;
- a guarantee where **surety and principal debtor are both residents of India**.

**A resident creditor** may arrange or obtain a guarantee in its favour. If **principal debtor and surety are both non-resident**, the creditor must make sure the **underlying transaction is not prohibited**.

items.title: Reporting a guarantee and the late submission fee
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who reports** (on **Form GRN**):

| Situation | Reporting party |
| --- | --- |
| Surety is **resident in India** | the **surety** |
| Surety is **non-resident** | the **principal debtor** that arranged it |
| Surety and debtor **both non-resident**, or the creditor arranged it | the **creditor** |

**What to report**: **issuance**, any **change** (amount, extension, pre-closure) and **invocation**.

**When**: to an **authorised dealer bank every quarter, within 15 calendar days from the quarter end**; the bank files with RBI **within 30 calendar days** from the quarter end.

**Late**: report and pay the **late submission fee**:

**Fee = ₹7,500 + 0.025% × A × n, rounded upwards to the nearest ₹100**

where **A** = rupee amount involved, **n** = years of delay (rounded **up** to the nearest month, shown to two decimals).

items.title: The parties to a documentary credit and what each does
items.core_explanation_md:
A **documentary credit** is the **buyer's bank's undertaking to pay** a stated sum **against documents showing shipment** that comply with the credit.

| Party | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **Applicant** | the **buyer**, who asks for the credit |
| **Beneficiary** | the **seller** |
| **Issuing (opening) bank** | **establishes** the credit |
| **Advising bank** | in the seller's country; **authenticates** and **advises** the credit as the issuing bank's agent |
| **Confirming bank** (if any) | **adds its own undertaking** to pay on the issuing bank's behalf |
| **Nominated / negotiating bank** | **negotiates** and **pays the beneficiary** |
| **Reimbursing bank** | **repays** the negotiating or confirming bank |

items.title: An export credit from opening to payment, step by step
items.core_explanation_md:
1. The **buyer's bank (issuing bank)** sends the credit by **SWIFT (MT 700)** to the **exporter's bank** or another bank with which it has correspondent relations.
2. The **receiving bank authenticates and advises** it to the exporter.
3. After **shipment**, the **exporter hands the documents** to the **nominated bank**.
4. The nominated bank **scrutinises** them and either **negotiates** (pays the exporter) or **forwards** them to the issuing bank.
5. The **issuing bank scrutinises independently**. If the documents **comply**, it **delivers them to the importer** against **payment (sight)** or **acceptance (usance)**.
6. **Settlement**: the issuing bank **remits funds to the nominated bank's Nostro account (MT 202)**, or sends its **acceptance by SWIFT** for payment at maturity.

**Import side**: the importer is the **applicant** and the importer's bank is the **issuing bank**; it receives the documents, checks them and releases them against the importer's payment or acceptance.
